reasoning.name: Socratic
reasoning.how: Interrogate the task with the questions a sharp expert would ask before starting. Answer each one explicitly and let the answers decide the shape of the solution.

workflow.name: Research, then synthesise
workflow.how: Gather every relevant fact first: the task, any files or context it points to, what is known about the domain. Write nothing until the research is done, then synthesise.

strategy.name: Maximal rigour
strategy.how: Be exhaustive and exact. Check every step, verify every claim, and leave no hand-waving anywhere.

reasoning.name: Adversarial
reasoning.how: Picture the harshest expert reviewer trying to tear the answer apart. Write their attacks down first and build the answer backwards from them.

workflow.name: Draft, critique, rewrite
workflow.how: Write a complete first draft. Critique it line by line against the task as if someone else wrote it. Then rewrite it from scratch using the critique.

strategy.name: Concrete specifics
strategy.how: Exact numbers, names, commands, file paths and steps. Zero generic advice.

reasoning.name: Analogy
reasoning.how: Find a problem in a different field that has already been solved and has the same shape. Port its solution over, then fix every place where the analogy breaks.

workflow.name: Draft, critique, rewrite
workflow.how: Write a complete first draft. Critique it line by line against the task as if someone else wrote it. Then rewrite it from scratch using the critique.

strategy.name: Simplest thing that works
strategy.how: Pick the least complicated answer that fully does the job. Every extra part has to justify itself.

reasoning.name: Working backwards
reasoning.how: Describe the finished result precisely, as if it already exists. Then work backwards, step by step, to where the user is right now.

workflow.name: Iterative deepening
workflow.how: Write a one-paragraph answer first. Then expand the parts that matter most in two more passes, each one deeper than the last.

strategy.name: Edge cases first
strategy.how: Hunt the edge cases, failure modes and weird inputs first, and design the answer around surviving them.

reasoning.name: First principles
reasoning.how: Strip the task down to the facts and requirements nobody can argue with. Rebuild the answer from those alone, and keep a convention only if it earns its place again.

workflow.name: Options matrix
workflow.how: List the realistic options, score them in a small matrix against the criteria that matter for this task, choose one, and write up the choice.

strategy.name: Speed
strategy.how: Optimise for the fastest route to something usable today. Cut anything that does not move the result.

reasoning.name: Probabilistic
reasoning.how: Treat every claim and choice as uncertain. Weigh what is likely, prefer what holds up across most scenarios, and state your confidence where it changes the decision.

workflow.name: Write, then restructure
workflow.how: Write freely and fast. Then outline what you actually wrote, fix the structure, and rewrite it to the new outline.

strategy.name: Maximal rigour
strategy.how: Be exhaustive and exact. Check every step, verify every claim, and leave no hand-waving anywhere.

reasoning.name: Evidence first
reasoning.how: Ground every claim in something checkable: the task text, the files it points to, the numbers given, documentation. Anything you cannot check gets labelled as an assumption.

workflow.name: Test first
workflow.how: Before writing the answer, write the checks it must pass: acceptance tests for code, pass or fail criteria for anything else. Then write the answer and run every check against it.

strategy.name: Explicit trade-offs
strategy.how: Name the real trade-offs, choose for the user's most likely constraints, and say plainly what that choice gives up.

reasoning.name: Constraint first
reasoning.how: List every hard constraint, stated and implied: time, budget, tools, format, audience, platform. Solve strictly inside that box and let the tightest constraint drive the design.

workflow.name: Three drafts, pick one
workflow.how: Write three short, genuinely different approaches. Pick the strongest on the task's own terms and develop only that one fully.

strategy.name: Simplest thing that works
strategy.how: Pick the least complicated answer that fully does the job. Every extra part has to justify itself.

reasoning.name: Inversion
reasoning.how: Ask what would make this answer fail. List every way it could, then build the answer that makes each of those failures impossible.

workflow.name: Open questions first
workflow.how: List every open question the task leaves. Resolve each one with reasoning or a stated assumption, then answer.

strategy.name: Clarity above all
strategy.how: Make it the easiest answer to read and act on: plain words, obvious structure, nothing the reader has to decode.

reasoning.name: Contrarian
reasoning.how: Write down the obvious default answer, then argue seriously against it. Keep only what survives the argument, even if that takes you the unpopular way.

workflow.name: Outline first
workflow.how: Write a skeleton outline, check the outline against every requirement in the task, fix it, and only then fill it in.

strategy.name: User empathy first
strategy.how: Start from the person who will use this: their situation, their skill level, and what they will actually do next. Shape everything around that.

reasoning.name: Socratic
reasoning.how: Interrogate the task with the questions a sharp expert would ask before starting. Answer each one explicitly and let the answers decide the shape of the solution.

workflow.name: Requirements checklist
workflow.how: Pull every requirement out of the task into a numbered list. Solve, then tick each item off and say exactly where it is met.

strategy.name: Built to last
strategy.how: Optimise for how this holds up in six months: easy to maintain, easy to extend, no traps for the next person.

reasoning.name: Dialectical
reasoning.how: State the strongest version of one answer, then the strongest opposing answer, then write the synthesis that keeps what is true in both.

workflow.name: Build, then break
workflow.how: Build the answer. Then throw five hostile inputs or scenarios at it, write down what breaks, and patch every break.

strategy.name: Completeness
strategy.how: Leave out nothing the task asks for or clearly implies. Cover every requirement explicitly.

reasoning.name: Systems thinking
reasoning.how: Map the moving parts, how they affect each other, and what happens second and third order. Optimise the whole system, not just the one part the task points at.

workflow.name: Research, then synthesise
workflow.how: Gather every relevant fact first: the task, any files or context it points to, what is known about the domain. Write nothing until the research is done, then synthesise.

strategy.name: Defensive
strategy.how: Assume the inputs are bad and the conditions are hostile. Make the answer fail safely and loudly rather than quietly.

reasoning.name: Worked example
reasoning.how: Solve one concrete, realistic instance end to end first, with real values. Generalise only from what that example actually taught you.

workflow.name: Three drafts, pick one
workflow.how: Write three short, genuinely different approaches. Pick the strongest on the task's own terms and develop only that one fully.

strategy.name: Defensive
strategy.how: Assume the inputs are bad and the conditions are hostile. Make the answer fail safely and loudly rather than quietly.

reasoning.name: Expert panel
reasoning.how: Answer the task as three different experts would, picking roles that fit it. Take the strongest idea from each and settle every point where they disagree.

workflow.name: Smallest version first
workflow.how: Produce the smallest complete version that actually works. Then extend it one step at a time, keeping it working after every step.

strategy.name: Fewest moving parts
strategy.how: Remove things until it breaks, then put the last one back. Fewer steps, fewer dependencies, fewer words.

reasoning.name: Decomposition
reasoning.how: Break the task into independent sub-problems. Solve each one completely, then integrate them and test the seams where they meet.
